subject: mcc-health-promotion
title: Hypertension screening: finding and confirming raised blood pressure

steps.tx: Hypertension is often **silent**, so screening means checking **blood pressure** opportunistically at routine contacts with clinicians. One elevated reading is never a diagnosis on its own. Under **NICE** guidance, a raised clinic value prompts confirmation, typically with **ambulatory** or **home monitoring**, before any treatment decision. The aim is detecting disease early, ideally before **target organ damage** appears.

steps.tx: Accurate **measurement technique** matters before any diagnosis. The patient should sit quietly for about five minutes with the back supported and feet flat. Choose a **cuff** whose bladder suits the arm circumference, because an undersized cuff overestimates pressure. Take at least two readings a minute apart and average them.

rows: Arm bare and at heart level

steps.tx: Once a clinic reading is raised, confirmation relies on **ambulatory blood pressure monitoring** or **home blood pressure monitoring**. Both average many readings across daily life, which limits the artefact of a single visit. Out-of-office averages are compared against lower diagnostic thresholds than clinic readings. Only **sustained elevation** confirms the diagnosis, so one high value is never enough.

steps.tx: Screen for **secondary hypertension** only when clues are present. Low potassium without diuretic use, especially with raised bicarbonate, points towards primary aldosteronism, tested by the aldosterone to renin ratio. Episodic headache with sweating or palpitations raises suspicion of a phaeochromocytoma, tested by metanephrines.

steps.tx: Baseline **end-organ** screening looks for damage and co-risk. A **urine albumin to creatinine ratio** finds early kidney injury, even when serum creatinine is normal. A **12-lead ECG** can reveal **left ventricular hypertrophy**. Fasting glucose or HbA1c flags **diabetes** as a co-risk, which changes treatment targets and urgency.
steps.say: Baseline end-organ screening looks for damage and co-risk. A urine albumin to creatinine ratio finds early kidney injury, even when serum creatinine is normal. A twelve-lead ECG can reveal left ventricular hypertrophy. Fasting glucose or HbA1c flags diabetes as a co-risk, which changes treatment targets and urgency.

steps.tx: Compare the two measurement methods. A **clinic reading** is a single snapshot and can be inflated by anxiety, the white coat effect. Home or ambulatory measurements average many readings and reflect the true sustained load. Use the averaged result, not one visit, to decide whether to treat.
